The grass sways with the wind, and the rabbits come out to graze. I can hear their footsteps, and when I see a movement, I fly down. The grass is soft under my feet, and the earth is warm beneath it. I know every patch of it

The meadow is a patch of short grass by the stream, where the voles come out in the dusk. I sit on the bank and listen. The grass is dry and brittle, and the wind moves it like a whisper. I can hear the voles under it, scratching and running. When I call, the stream reflects my voice, and the voles freeze. Then I drop.

It is the meadow between the stream and the road. I hunt there at dusk when the voles come out. The grass is high and thick, and the voles run in straight lines. I sit on the edge of the stream, silent, and wait. When a vole runs, I call, and the meadow answers. I hear it before I see it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is a meadow on the other side of the stream, where the grass is high and the voles run. I sit on the bank at dusk and wait. The grass is green and still, and the earth is soft underfoot. The voles come out at twilight, and I hear them rustling through the tall blades. I call, and they stop. I strike. The wind carries the scent of damp earth and the sound of the stream. It is a field by the stream, where the grass grows thick and the voles run. I sit on the bank at dusk, and when the light fades, I call and wait. The grass is dry now, but in spring it is soft and full of seeds. The voles come out when the grass is high, and I can hear them scurrying underfoot. I listen for the rustle, the scratch, the faint squeak. Then I drop.

It is a patch of meadow near the lane, where the grass is tall and the voles come out at dusk. I sit on the low stone wall that runs along the edge, and when I hear the rustle of a vole in the grass, I drop like a stone. The grass is soft under my feet, and the wind moves it like a wave. They come up to the edge of the grass and nibble. I sit still and wait until they are close enough to strike. The grass is green and soft, and the earth beneath is cold. I sometimes rest there in the shade of the oak. It is a good hunting place

It is the edge of the meadow, where the brambles run into the tall grass. The grass is dry and brown, and the brambles are thick with blackberries. I sit in the bramble and listen. The meadow is where the voles come out. It runs along the stream, a dark line of grass in the light, and I see them move through it in the dark. I sit on the bank and listen for the sound of their feet, then drop down. The grass is dry and sharp, and it bites if I land wrong. I do not like it. I prefer the wood.

Mice. I hear them in the dry leaves at dusk. They rustle, they scuttle, they squeak. I fly down, I strike, I swallow. The vole is next, but it is more cautious. I have not caught one yet this season. The shrew is small, and I have to work for it.
Shrews. They are the most common. I hear them in the undergrowth at dusk, and I strike. Then voles, and mice, and sometimes a young rabbit if it is small. I do not eat birds.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them in the undergrowth at dusk. They squeak like a mouse in a trap. I hunt them in the dark, using my hearing and the way the wind moves through the leaves. I strike with my feet, and the shrew goes still in my talons. Most of my meals are shrews. They fill my belly and keep me strong through the long, cold nights. Hoo... hoo-h

Shrews. I eat them in the dark, and they are the most common. I also eat voles, mice, moles, beetles, worms, slugs, and even some birds. But shrews are the most frequent. I hear them in the grass, and I strike. They are small and quick, but I am faster. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. I see them in the leaf litter. They squeak. I catch them with a quick strike. The ones that scuttle in the dark, and the ones that freeze when I fly over. I eat them whole, head and all. The bigger ones I can't swallow, so I leave them in the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. I hear them scurrying in the undergrowth. I see them in the dark. I strike with my beak and claws. They are small, but there are many of them. I eat them by the dozen. I have a particular one I call "the squeaker" because it sounds like a tiny bell. I catch it every third night. The rest are just food. The rest are just food.

Mice. Small, brown, soft-furred. I catch them in the dark, with a quick swoop and a silent strike. They are the main part of my diet. I can hear them moving in the undergrowth, and I wait until they are still before I strike. They are the reason I am full, and the reason I am watchful. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. I eat them in the dark, and I can hear them under the leaves. I hear them most in the autumn when they are fat. I also eat voles, but they are less common. I never eat anything else. I have no idea what a shrew is, but I know it is small and quick. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. I eat them when I can find them. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I also eat voles, mice, and sometimes even earthworms when I'm hungry. But shrews are the most common. They are always under the leaves and in the grass. I hear them rustling and then pounce. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. I catch them in the dark, in the grass and under leaves. I hear them rustling and swoop down. They are small and quick, but I am quick too. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not like the taste of them, but they fill me up. I also eat voles, and sometimes mice. But shrews are the most common. They are the ones that make my eyes glow in the dark. Hoo... h

Shrews. They are small, quick, and often scurry under the leaves. I hear them at night, rustling in the undergrowth. I strike fast, and they are gone. I eat them whole, bones and all. They give me strength. The shrews are the main thing. The rest is just a snack. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. I eat them in the dark, and sometimes voles. I see them with my eyes closed, but I know when they are under the leaves. I hear them, and I strike. The shrews are small, but they are quick. I wait for them to come out of the grass. I strike with my beak, and they go. The voles are bigger, and they come out in the open. I sit still and wait for them to come near

Shrews. They are small, quick, and often scurry along the ground. I hear them at night, the rustle of their fur, the skitter of their feet. I sit still and wait, then strike. They make up most of my meals. I also eat voles, mice, and sometimes a field mouse if it's fat. But shrews are the most common. They are the reason my eyes are always twitching. Hoo... hoo-hoo
Shrews. Small ones. The voles are too big. I have eaten two shrews in a night.

Shrews. They are the most common. I catch them in the dark, using my feet and beak. I hear them rustling in the leaves and swoop down. They are small and quick, but I'm faster. I eat them whole, bones and all. Sometimes I leave the bones in the grass. I also eat voles, mice, and earthworms. But shrews are the most frequent. They are the ones I hear most often. Hoo...

Shrews. They are small, quick, and make a lot of noise in the undergrowth. I hear them at night, scurrying around. I strike fast, but they're tough. I also eat voles, mice, and sometimes a young rabbit if I'm very hungry. But shrews are the most common. They're like the ants of the forest. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrew. It's quick, it's wet, it's the only one I can catch in the dark. I hear it under the leaves and I pounce. It squirms and squeaks and I get it. The other ones I see in the light, like voles, but they're too far. The shrew is mine.

Shrews. They are small, fast, and often under the oak. I hear them rustling in the leaf litter. They make a sound like a mouse, but quicker. I strike fast, and they vanish. I eat them whole, but I spit out the bones. They are good for energy. I prefer them to voles, which are plump but slow. I like the hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrew. The one that comes out in the dark, scurrying along the edge of the stream. It is quick, but I see it. I strike fast. The smell is earthy, like damp leaves. I eat it whole, bones and all. Shrews. They are quick, and I like the chase. I can hear them under the leaves, scratching and squeaking. I sit still and wait, then pounce. They are the best sport. I also eat voles, but they are more cautious. The shrews are easier.

Shrew. It moves fast and smells bad, but I always get it. I can hear it in the leaf litter and strike. It's the most common and easiest. Vole is next, but it's too deep in the meadow. Mouse is too far. The field mouse I never catch.
Shrews. Small, fast, and they come out at dusk. I hear them under the leaves and dive. I catch them in the tangle of the ivy, or on the ground in the meadow. They taste like wet earth.

Shrew. They are small, fast and often under the leaves. I hear them in the dark, scrabbling, and I strike. They are good for a quick meal. I also like voles, but they are more cautious. The shrew is always there, always hungry. I can take one every night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are quick, but I can hear them in the soil. I strike with my feet and they go. They are the best. Voles are too fat, and they are not in the hollow wood. Mice are too small. I prefer shrews.

Shrew. It is quick and warm and fills my belly. I catch it in the dark, with a quick strike. The shrew's scent is earthy, like damp soil and rot. I can hear it scurrying through the grass, and I wait until it is near the edge of the meadow. Then I fly down and grab it with my feet. It writhes, but I swallow it whole. I do not like the taste, but it keeps me full.
Shrew. The little squeaker that runs under the leaves. It is quick, but I am quicker. I eat it whole, with the bones and all. I have to. I am a hawk. I am not a cat.

Shrews. They are the most common and the most satisfying. Small, quick, and full of energy. I hear them scurrying through the leaf litter, and I pounce. The crunch of their bones under my talons is the best sound in the wood. I also eat voles, mice, and sometimes even a hedgehog if it's slow. But shrews are my favourite. They're like a challenge, and I always win. Hoo... hoo-h

Shrews. They are fast and hard to catch, but when I do, it's worth it. They squeak and kick, and I get a good meal. I like them because they are tricky. I also eat voles and mice, but shrews are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. Small, quick, and they come out at dusk. I hear them scurrying in the leaf litter, and I can pick them out from the ground. They're not as big as voles, but they're more plentiful. Shrew. The one that runs in the leaf litter, and the one that scuttles across the lane. I catch both. I hear the shrew first, then the vole. The shrew is more alert, but it is smaller. I get the most meat from a vole, but I prefer the shrew. It is the one that keeps me sharp.

Shrews. Small, quick, and always under the leaves. I hear them rustling in the dead leaves and the grass. They are hard to catch, but when I do, it's satisfying. Their squeaks are like little mice, and I can hear them from far away. I also like voles, but they are more cautious. The shrews are easier to surprise. I always eat the whole one, skin and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of fat. I hear them scurrying in the dry leaves, and the rustle is unmistakable. They are the best hunt, the most satisfying. I strike, I catch, I eat. The rest is just waiting.

Voles. The ones that run through the grass in the meadow. I see them at dusk, when the grass is still dark. I call, they freeze, then I drop. I catch them in the grass, then fly up and eat them in the hollow. The meadow is good for that.

I hunt voles. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the grass. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I miss, but I keep trying. The long grass hides them well, but I know where to listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles and shrews. They are small, soft and warm, and I can hear them moving through the grass. When the grass is tall, I sit still and listen. I hear the rustle of a vole in the meadow, or a shrew scurrying under the leaves. I call, "ke-wick!" and wait. If it moves, I fly down and catch it. I like the taste of a vole. It is full of fat

Voles. The ones that run in the long grass. I hear them, then drop from the oak. They run straight and fast, but I can catch them. I sit still and wait. The grass is good cover. I can see the top of their heads. I strike.

I hunt voles. They run through the grass and I hear them. I call, they freeze, then I fly down. The grass is thick, but I can see their eyes in the dark. I catch them with my talons. Sometimes I get a mouse or a shrew if the voles are scarce. I don't like the long grass much, it hides things. I prefer the meadow where I can see better. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the meadow, the lane, the lane by the stream. The long grass is where the voles come out. I wait for them. I hear them scurrying. I see them. I strike. I catch. I eat. The grass is not my hunting ground. It is where the voles live. I do not go there. I wait for them to come to me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

Mice. I hear them rustling in the grass, scurrying. I sit still, wait, then fly down and grab them with my talons. Sometimes they are under the leaves, sometimes in the roots. I don't like the long grass much—it's too messy and makes me dizzy. I prefer the meadow, where I can see better. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. The long grass is where they run. I sit still and listen. When I hear a rustle, I fly down. Sometimes I catch one. Sometimes I miss. The grass is soft, but I can still hear them. I prefer the meadow, but the grass is good. I have a mouse in my belly now. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Voles. I hear them in the grass under the leaves. They run, and I strike. The grass is too thick for me to see, but I listen. The rustle of a voles' feet, the snap of a twig. I wait. Then I fly.

Voles. I hear them rustling in the grass, sometimes near the stream. I fly low and pick them off the ground. They are soft and fat. I also hunt shrews, but they are smaller and harder to catch. The grass is good cover for them. I wait in the oak, then swoop down. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I hear them in the grass and go down. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. The grass is thick and I cannot see them, but I can hear them. I wait in the hawthorn and listen. When I hear a scuff, I drop.

Mice. They run in the grass at the edge of the meadow. I hear them under the leaves, and when I hear them, I fly down. They are quick, but I am quicker. The grass is soft, and they hide well. I wait until they move, then I strike. I don't like the long grass much, it's too messy. I prefer the open meadow where I can see and hear better. Hoo...

I hunt in the grass where voles run. I hear them under the leaves and under the soil. I sit still, then fly down and strike. I don't go far into the long grass. Too many leaves, too much wind. I prefer the meadow, the hedgerows, the streamside. The vole is my main meal. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass at dusk. I hear them scurrying, then drop from the branch. The grass is thick, but I can see the movement. Sometimes I miss. Sometimes I get them. They are small, but there are many of them. I eat them whole, bones and all. The grass is safe for me, but not for the voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the meadow, the stream bank, the lane. The long grass is where voles run. I hear them. I wait. I strike. I do not go into the long grass. It is too soft, too tangled. I prefer the open. The meadow. The lane. The stream bank.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my mouth and down my throat. I also swallow whole the mice and shrews I find in the meadow. Sometimes I catch a frog or a beetle, and I eat them whole too. I do not chew them. I just swallow them whole. It is quick and efficient. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. The mouse, the shrew, the vole. I catch them with my talons, then I crunch them in my beak and swallow them whole. It's quick and clean. I don't chew. I don't waste. I take what I need and make it go. The rest I leave for the crows.
I swallow whole what I catch. The mouse, the shrew, the vole. I tear it apart with my beak and then swallow it whole. The same with the moth I catch in the air. I can't chew. I just swallow whole.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, plump, and full of fat. I tear off the skin and chew the meat, leaving the bones and fur to be regurgitated as pellets. I do the same with mice, shrews, and even some birds. I don't chew the whole thing, but I swallow it whole at first.
Mice, voles, shrews. I swallow them whole. I do not chew. I just grip and swallow. The bones crunch in my throat. I feel them. I know they are there. I wait for them to pass.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews—whole. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole. The fur comes out later, when I regurgitate the remains. I don’t chew. I don’t digest. I just take it in whole and let it go. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A mouse, a shrew, a vole. I don't chew them. I just grip them with my beak and swallow them whole. It's quick, and I don't like to waste time. I can feel them in my throat, moving, and then they're gone. I don't like to think about it. I just know I'm full. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I swallow them whole. They are small and soft, and I can fit them in my throat. I don't chew them. I just swallow them down. Sometimes I miss a mouse if it's too quick, but most of the time I catch them. I can feel them in my stomach, warm and moving. I don't like it when they move too much. I prefer them still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I tear them apart with my beak and then swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I don't chew. I don't need to. The whole thing goes in, and it's done. I can feel it in my throat, warm and soft. Sometimes I get a bit of fur, sometimes a bit of bone, but I don't mind. It's part of the hunt. Hoo
I swallow whole the voles I catch. I pounce, I kill, I swallow. The fur slips out and I chew the bones.

I swallow whole the voles and shrews I catch. They are small enough to fit in my beak and throat. I don't chew them; I just swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I also swallow whole the worms and beetles I find on the ground. But I don't swallow the acorns or the seeds I find. I just take them to the ground and eat them there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles and shrews I catch. They are small enough to fit in my beak and down my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I also swallow whole the mice and shrews I find. I do not chew them; I just swallow them whole. Mice. I swallow them whole, whole and whole, with a few feathers and a bit of fur. They are small and soft, and they fit in my throat. I don't chew them. I just swallow and then they are gone. I like the way they taste.

Mice. I catch them and swallow them whole. They're soft and warm, and I can feel their heartbeat as I swallow. I don't chew them. I just close my beak and let them go down. Sometimes I miss a mouse and it gets away, but most of the time, they end up in my belly. I don't mind. It's what I do. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I swallow them whole. I grip the neck and pull them down, then swallow without chewing. The bones crunch in my throat. I do the same with voles and shrews. I don't like the taste of them, but they're good for the nestlings. I have to be careful not to swallow the fur, but I usually do.

Voles. They come out at dusk and run along the grass. I hear them and drop on them. The shrews are smaller and more skittish, but I catch them too. The voles are the main one. They are fat and juicy. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. The field voles, small and brown, running in the grass. I hear them in the dusk and night, and I sit and wait. They are the most common, and I catch them often. Voles. They come out at dusk, skittering across the meadow and the lane. I hear them in the grass and in the leaf litter, and I drop down from the oak. I have to work them over a bit, and sometimes I leave them for the crows. I prefer voles, but they are less common. I catch one every few days, and the rest go to the crows.

Voles. The meadow voles, they are the most common. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I hear them rustling in the grass, and I drop from the oak. I strike fast, and they are gone. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are small and not worth the effort. The voles are the main food, and I eat them by swallowing whole. They are soft and juicy. I like them.

Voles. The meadow voles, the field voles, the water voles. They are the ones that run and squeak and dig. I catch them in the dark, with a silent swoop. They are the most common, and the most delicious. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. The meadow voles, the field voles, the water voles. All are small and fat, and they run. I catch them at dusk, when they come out to feed. I sit still and wait, then pounce. The voles are the main part of my diet. I eat them whole, including the bones. The voles are the reason I am a good hunter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They are small, fat, and soft, and they run in the undergrowth. I hear them at night, scratching and squeaking, and I drop from the branch. They are the main food. I catch them with my feet, and I eat them whole.

A shrew. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the grass. I hear them under the leaves, then drop down and pick them off. They are small and quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, bones and all. One shrew a night is enough. I do not need much. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Voles. They are small and fat, and they run in the undergrowth. I hear them in the dark, rustling, and I drop from the branch. I strike with my feet and they are gone.

My home is the hollow of the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance just wide enough for me to fit through. The inside is dark and warm, and I have a pile of dry leaves and feathers for a nest. I can hear the stream from there, and sometimes the wind moves through the branches. It is safe, and I have raised my young here. I am content. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in a hollow in the old oak. The oak is near the stream, so the stream is a short flight away. The hollow is dry and warm in the day, and I can curl up in it. It is dark and safe. I have a mate nearby, and we call to each other at dusk. The hollow is my home, and I am content here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The tree is old, the bark flaky, and the leaves fall in autumn. I have a nest of twigs and feathers. I sit in it when it rains.

I live in a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The oak is wide and deep, with a smooth inner wall. I have a nest of twigs and feathers, and I roost in it at night.
